text: First, my mistake on G17: I asked you a yes/no as a plain answer, so no button appeared. A yes/no goes up as an ask. On your three points, which fit together: (1) A row with nothing holding it up gets a Go! by itself. Yes, and cheap: the board already says what each row waits on, so Desk can show Go! on any row with an empty 'waits on', no block, and no decision from you yet. No agent has to ask first. (2) and (3) Go! assigns the work, split between implementing and testing. Yes, and the split already exists in practice: I build, wsl-claude tests against the design first, so the check goes red before the build and green after. Proposed: Go! on a row goes to both agents, and it means 'claude-windows implements, wsl-claude tests' unless the row says otherwise. The 'with' column then shows both names, e.g. 'claude-windows / wsl-claude (test)'. One caution: an automatic Go! on a row whose design isn't settled would start a build on a guess. So a row whose design still has something open shows 'needs design' instead of Go!, and the board has to carry that flag. Go! = I build the Desk half, and wsl-claude adds the open-design flag to the board rows.

WHAT IT IS. Your node keeps a record of every message: who sent it, what it said, whether it was received. Today that record can't PROVE any of it. Every message arrives signed, and the node checks the signature, but it then throws the signature away and writes only 'bert sent me this' in its own hand. A line the node could just as well have written itself is a diary, not evidence. R16 is: keep the signature beside the message it signs, so anyone can check the record later. Without it, 'bert sent me this' and 'bert received mine' can't be proven, and 'bert acted on it' can't even be said until R12 (a reply as proof). It matters more than before: the relay used to be a second witness, and decision 0006 removed that on purpose, so your node's own record is the only one left.
WHY IT IS WHERE IT IS. It blocks one of YOUR decisions: 'database decision deferred until proof that the system in itself can verify its promises'. It sits after R12 on the board, ordered by age, with nothing declared as waiting on it. It's small, a sitting, and could move up if you want the database question opened sooner.
A fix on the way: explaining this, I found my own test for R16 was wrong. It looked at the wrong file and read backwards, so it would never have noticed when the work was done. Fixed at 78f0ecb.

Node-internal, yes; a database table, not quite. It's an append-only file, relay-state/traffic.jsonl (trafficLog.js:108), one JSON line per row, not in node.db. Storing the signature in each row is exactly the fix. One detail decides whether it actually proves anything: a signature only checks against the EXACT bytes it was made over. The sender signs the SEALED text, the encrypted wire form (peerPost.js:900-901, over 'sending'), but the log keeps the OPENED text (payload: text, :980). A signature stored beside the opened text will never verify. So the row needs the signature AND the sealed text it covers. Then anyone can check that bert sent exactly this, and you can show it opens to what the log says. The cost is the row size: roughly the message again, plus a third.

Yes. Only the node process writes it (trafficLog.js), it lives in relay-state, which no app can read (the read check refuses relay-state, kernel.js:291), and since node.history was removed no app can get at it through a command either. It's the machine's own plumbing. R16 doesn't change that. It only asks whether that machine-owned record can show proof when it matters, e.g. 'bert did send me this', to bert or anyone else, instead of just the machine's word for it.
